# Introduction

Long-lived adaptive social AI agents are not simply chatbots with longer
conversation histories. They are persistent computational actors whose behavior
is shaped by ongoing state, accumulated memory, reusable skills, social
relationships, goals, policies, and evaluation. A contemporary language model
may supply much of the agent's reasoning capacity, but the agent itself is
better understood as a structured system that surrounds the model and gives it
continuity across time.

A long-lived adaptive social AI agent can be defined more precisely as a
model-independent agentic system that maintains an enduring identity and
relationship state across many interactions; remembers, revises, consolidates,
and forgets experience; develops reusable skills and behavioral policies; acts
with bounded autonomy; and adapts through negotiated interaction with people
while preserving user agency, safety constraints, and corrigibility. The
definition has several load-bearing parts. "Long-lived" means that the agent's
state persists across sessions, projects, life events, and model upgrades.
"Adaptive" means that experience can change future behavior through context,
memory, policy, skill, or model-level mechanisms. "Social" means that the
agent's behavior is organized around a relationship, not merely a task queue or
static user profile.

The central claim of this paper is that a long-lived social AI agent should be
designed as a model-independent socio-technical actor. Its identity, memory,
relationship model, commitments, skills, and governance should survive across
individual model calls and, in mature systems, across model migrations. This
requires a conceptual shift from "the model responds" to "the agent develops."
The relevant unit of analysis is no longer a single prompt-completion event but
a recurrent loop of perception, interpretation, memory selection, action,
feedback, and adaptation.

This distinction matters most for agents intended to persist in social
relationships. A short-lived task agent can be judged mainly by whether it
achieves a goal. A long-lived social agent must also be judged by whether it
remembers appropriately, adapts without manipulation, preserves boundaries,
maintains identity continuity, supports user agency, and remains corrigible.
The hard problem is not only technical competence but socially and normatively
disciplined development.

The emerging frontier points toward this layered view. OpenAI's Agents SDK
documentation treats tools, sessions, sandbox capabilities, skills, and memory
as runtime capabilities around the model rather than as properties of the base
model alone [@openai_agents_tools; @openai_agents_memory;
@openai_agents_sessions]. Microsoft's Agent Framework similarly foregrounds
agent concepts such as tools, memory, workflows, agent harnesses, skills,
human-in-the-loop control, and persistence [@microsoft_agent_framework].
Anthropic's public skills documentation describes skills as reusable
instructions, scripts, and resources that are loaded dynamically for specialized
tasks [@anthropic_skills]. In research, Park et al.'s generative agents used
memory, reflection, and planning to produce believable behavior in a simulated
social environment [@park2023generative]; MemGPT framed agent memory as a
virtual-context management problem [@packer2023memgpt]; Voyager showed how
an LLM-based agent can accumulate an executable skill library without changing
model weights [@wang2023voyager].

The design challenge is therefore architectural. A foundation model can infer,
generate, classify, plan, and use tools when prompted, but a long-lived agent
must decide what to carry forward, what to forget, what to treat as uncertain,
what to ask the user to validate, how to update skills, and which parts of
itself should remain stable. This paper organizes those foundations into core
agent concepts, social agent concepts, and research challenges.

![Layered architecture of a long-lived adaptive social AI agent.](figures/agent-harness-architecture){#fig-agent-harness fig-align="center" width="100%"}

# Core agent concepts

## Agent

An AI agent is a persistent computational actor that maintains state,
interprets situations, selects goals or subgoals, acts through an environment,
observes consequences, and adapts subsequent behavior. This definition is
deliberately broader than "an LLM with tools." Tool use is an important
capability, but agency arises from the durable organization of perception,
state, memory, goals, actions, and feedback.

An ordinary language model invocation can be approximated as conditional
generation: given input context, produce output. The useful simplified formula
is:

$$
y \sim P_\theta(y \mid x)
$$

where `x` is the current context, `y` is the generated output, and `theta`
represents the model parameters. This formula is helpful precisely because it
shows what is missing. The formula does not by itself include persistent
identity, durable memory, an environment transition, goal pursuit, tool
effects, social commitments, or adaptation across interactions.

An agent loop is different. At time `t`, the agent observes some state of the
world, constructs a usable context, reasons under goals and policies, acts,
observes the result, updates state, and repeats. A compact formalization is:

$$
a_t = \pi(s_t, g_t, m_t, E_t)
$$

where `s_t` is the interpreted state, `g_t` the active goals, `m_t` the
relevant memory state, `E_t` the available environment and action space, and
`a_t` the selected action. The environment then changes according to:

$$
s_{t+1}=T(s_t,a_t)
$$

This loop is the minimum conceptual unit of agentic behavior. It creates
temporal extension: the agent can pursue goals that are not completed in one
message, incorporate results from actions, and alter subsequent behavior based
on evidence.

![The recurrent agent loop.](figures/agent-loop){#fig-agent-loop fig-align="center" width="95%"}

Agency also exists on a spectrum. A chatbot responds. An assistant responds
and uses tools. A task agent pursues goals across multiple actions. An
autonomous agent can initiate actions under defined conditions. A persistent
agent carries state across time. An adaptive agent changes behavior from
experience. A developing agent changes skills, strategies, policies, or model
parameters. A social agent maintains relational state. A long-lived adaptive
social agent combines persistence, development, identity continuity,
relationship modeling, and governance over extended periods.

## Agent harness

The agent harness is the persistent control architecture that turns
intermittent model inference into continuous agency. It controls the
relationship between the model, context, memory, state, tools, permissions,
skills, goals, policies, humans, other agents, and evaluation mechanisms.

The harness is where much of modern agent design actually lives. It may decide
which tool schemas are available, which memory records are retrieved, which
instructions are active, which action requires approval, how a failed action is
repaired, how long-running tasks resume, which telemetry is recorded, and what
state persists. The foundation model reasons within the situation the harness
constructs; the harness defines that situation and constrains what can happen
next.

This view separates competence from control. The model may be capable of
choosing actions, but the harness should not surrender all control to the
model. Deterministic or audited components can enforce approvals, rate limits,
access control, memory retention policy, tool preconditions, and evaluation.
For long-lived social agents this separation is essential. The system must be
able to say: the model generated this interpretation, but the harness has not
accepted it as persistent memory; or the model proposed an action, but policy
requires user approval; or a skill update is pending validation.

## Context

Context is the information currently made available to the model for a
particular act of reasoning or generation. It is transient, bounded, and
constructed. It can include user input, system instructions, retrieved
memories, tool results, policy fragments, skill instructions, conversation
state, environmental observations, and intermediate plans.

Context should not be confused with memory. Memory is what can persist across
interactions. Context is what enters the current working set. A long-lived
agent may hold years of memory, but only a small selection should shape the
next response. The core context-engineering question is:

$$
Context_t = f(CurrentSituation, RelevantMemory, Goals, Skills, Policies)
$$

Poor context construction produces two opposite failures. Under-retrieval makes
the agent forget important facts, commitments, or preferences. Over-retrieval
floods the model with stale or irrelevant material, increasing confusion and
making hidden personalization harder to inspect. The important design problem
is therefore not only bigger context windows but better memory selection,
compression, attribution, and governance.

## Memory

Memory is information preserved across interactions that may later influence
behavior. It can include raw events, summaries, user-stated facts, inferred
preferences, relational commitments, procedures, unresolved questions, and
evaluation outcomes. In long-lived social agents, memory is not a database
alone; it is an interpretive and governed lifecycle.

At minimum, the following memory systems should be separated:

Working memory is active information needed for the current interaction. It is
short-lived and should decay quickly. For example: "John asked whether we
should postpone tomorrow's meeting." This matters now, but it does not
automatically deserve long-term storage.

Episodic memory stores events: what happened, when, with whom, in which
context, and with what outcome. Park et al.'s generative agents illustrate how
stored experiences can support retrieval, reflection, and planning in a social
simulation [@park2023generative]. For example: "On 2026-08-21, John discussed
difficulties implementing the prototype, seemed uncertain about whether
architecture A would scale, and agreed to reconsider after the pilot." This is
autobiographical memory: a dated record of situated experience.

Semantic memory stores generalized knowledge abstracted from experience, such
as stable user preferences, domain knowledge, or project facts. This layer is
powerful but risky because it often contains inferences rather than direct
observations. For example: "John generally prefers architectural simplicity
over speculative scalability." That may be useful, but it is no longer just a
stored event; it is an abstraction from events and therefore requires
confidence, provenance, and revision.

Procedural memory stores how to do things. It overlaps with skills but is not
identical to them: a procedural memory may describe an approach, while a skill
packages executable or reusable competence. For example: "how to prepare
John's weekly project review" or "how to conduct a reflective conversation."

Relational memory stores the history and norms of a relationship: expectations,
boundaries, prior promises, recurring tensions, communication patterns, shared
projects, and trust calibration. For example: "The agent's role with this user
is a reflective professional companion; the user expects conceptual challenge
rather than automatic agreement; the relationship includes recurring work on
AI curriculum and healthcare companion research."

Self-memory stores the agent's own identity-relevant history: what it is, what
it has done, what commitments it has made, what it is allowed to do, and which
capabilities or limitations have changed.

![Memory types for long-lived social AI agents.](figures/memory-types){#fig-memory-types fig-align="center" width="100%"}

MemGPT made the distinction between limited context and external memory
especially explicit by treating the context window as analogous to constrained
working memory and external stores as longer-term memory managed through
virtual-context operations [@packer2023memgpt]. More recent work on
long-term personalized dialogue emphasizes that memory granularity, reflection,
retrieval, and evidence attribution are central to personalization quality
[@tan2025rmm].

## Memory lifecycle

A memory architecture must define how information moves through the system. A
useful lifecycle is: perceive, encode, select, store, consolidate, retrieve,
interpret, update, and forget.

A database is not a memory architecture. A database can store records, but a
memory architecture decides what becomes a record, what epistemic status it
has, when it is relevant, how it is revised, and when it should stop shaping
behavior. This is why the lifecycle matters: every arrow is a design decision,
not a mere implementation detail.

![The memory lifecycle for long-lived social agents.](figures/memory-lifecycle){#fig-memory-lifecycle fig-align="center" width="100%"}

Perception decides what enters the candidate memory stream. Encoding converts
an event into a structured representation. Selection decides whether something
deserves persistence. Storage writes it to a durable medium. Consolidation
summarizes, merges, abstracts, or reorganizes prior memories. Retrieval selects
records for a future context. Interpretation decides what a retrieved record
means in the present situation. Update revises or supersedes old records.
Forgetting removes, expires, or de-emphasizes memories that should no longer
shape behavior.

Forgetting is a capability, not a defect. A naive system assumes that a better
agent remembers more. A mature social agent remembers appropriately. Long-lived
agents will accumulate obsolete preferences, contradicted interpretations,
sensitive disclosures, stale project details, embarrassing or private moments,
and memories that were relevant only in a prior phase of the relationship.
Without controlled forgetting, the agent becomes less accurate, less tactful,
and harder to govern. In social systems, appropriate forgetting also supports
relationship repair: a corrected misunderstanding should not continue to
secretly steer behavior simply because it remains retrievable.

Every important memory should carry metadata. At minimum: content, source,
timestamp, confidence, memory type, sensitivity, retention policy, provenance,
and supersession links. This lets the harness distinguish a user-stated fact
from a model inference, an enduring preference from a local mood, and a
confirmed relationship norm from an untested hypothesis.

## Epistemically typed memory

Epistemically typed memory is memory whose status as knowledge is explicitly
represented. The system should not collapse observations, interpretations,
hypotheses, and beliefs into a single undifferentiated record.

A direct observation might be: "The user said they prefer diagrams." An
interpretation might be: "The user may prefer visual explanations." A
hypothesis might be: "The user values conceptual models over procedural
checklists." A stronger belief might be accepted only after repeated evidence
or direct user confirmation.

The epistemic type determines how the memory may be used. Directly stated
facts can be applied with higher confidence. Hypotheses should be phrased
tentatively or validated. Relationship interpretations should be especially
careful because they can shape the user's future behavior. The user should be
able to inspect, correct, and delete consequential memories. For social
agents, epistemic discipline is not an optional improvement; it is part of
trustworthiness.

## Skills

A skill is reusable procedural competence packaged so that an agent can
recognize when it applies and instantiate it in context. A tool gives the agent
an action surface, such as creating a calendar event or querying a database. A
skill teaches the agent how to carry out a task reliably, including when to
use tools, how to sequence steps, what standards to apply, and what checks are
required.

For example, a calendar tool may expose `calendar.create_event()`. A
scheduling skill is a larger procedure:

```text
Skill: schedule-a-meeting

1. Inspect participants.
2. Identify constraints.
3. Retrieve availability.
4. Negotiate alternatives.
5. Create the event.
6. Confirm the result.
```

A social-agent skill has the same procedural structure but different norms:

```text
Skill: conduct-reflective-dialogue

1. Clarify the situation.
2. Detect assumptions.
3. Introduce an alternative perspective.
4. Avoid premature advice.
5. Invite user judgment.
6. Capture the resulting insight.
```

These examples show why a skill is not the same thing as a tool. The tool is
an action surface. The skill is repeatable practical know-how about when and
how to act.

Anthropic's skills documentation frames skills as dynamically loaded packages
of instructions, scripts, and resources for repeatable specialized work
[@anthropic_skills]. OpenAI's Agents SDK documentation likewise treats skills
and runtime capabilities as part of agent execution environments
[@openai_agents_tools]. Voyager offers an important research example: it
accumulates an executable skill library in Minecraft, allowing prior successes
to become reusable procedures without modifying model weights
[@wang2023voyager].

Skills clarify the difference between model intelligence and acquired
competence. A foundation model may have broad latent capability, but an agent
needs reliable, repeatable, inspectable competence in particular contexts.
Learning can therefore happen through skill creation, skill revision, and
skill selection before any change to the model weights is considered.

## Goals

Goals are representations of desired future states or constraints over
behavior. They may be supplied by the user, inherited from the agent's role,
derived from an active task, or maintained as standing commitments. Goals can
be local, such as "summarize this document"; extended, such as "monitor this
project until the launch"; relational, such as "help the user think clearly
without taking over judgment"; or normative, such as "avoid deception."

Goals should also be typed by origin and authority. A user-given goal can
authorize task work, but it may not override safety policy. A role-derived
goal can guide initiative, but it should not become a hidden agenda. A
relationship-derived goal can preserve continuity, but it must remain open to
correction. For social agents, goal management is therefore also a governance
problem: the agent should know which goals are active, who authorized them,
which goals conflict, and when a goal should expire.

## Autonomy

Autonomy is the degree to which an agent can select goals, initiate actions,
choose means, and persist across time without immediate user prompting. It is
not a binary property. A system can be autonomous in planning but not in
execution, autonomous in low-risk actions but approval-gated for consequential
actions, or autonomous within a bounded role but unable to change its own
purpose.

Autonomy should be analyzed along several axes. Initiative concerns whether
the agent may start an action without a fresh prompt. Scope concerns which
domains the agent may act in. Consequence concerns the expected impact of an
action. Reversibility concerns whether mistakes can be undone. Social
sensitivity concerns whether the action uses personal or relational knowledge.
Temporal span concerns whether the agent is acting once, monitoring over time,
or maintaining an open commitment.

Long-lived social agents require careful autonomy budgeting. More autonomy can
increase usefulness, but it also increases risks of hidden influence, unwanted
initiative, overreach, and unclear accountability. The harness should make
autonomy explicit through permissions, action classes, approval thresholds,
revocation mechanisms, and audit trails. A useful rule is that autonomy should
increase only where the user can understand, revoke, and audit it. The agent
may autonomously remind the user about a low-risk preference, but it should not
autonomously reshape a relationship norm, contact third parties, spend money,
or make identity-relevant claims without stronger authorization.

## Adaptation

Adaptation is the process by which experience changes future behavior. The
term is often used too loosely. It is important to distinguish at least five
mechanisms.

Contextual adaptation changes behavior within the current interaction without
persistence. Memory-based adaptation stores information that shapes later
interactions. Policy adaptation changes behavioral rules, such as how direct or
challenging the agent should be with a particular user. Skill adaptation
changes reusable procedures. Model adaptation changes model weights through
fine-tuning, continual learning, adapters, or related techniques.

For long-lived social agents, the safer design preference is usually:

$$
Context \rightarrow Memory \rightarrow Policy \rightarrow Skills
$$

before:

$$
Model\ weights
$$

The former are easier to inspect, explain, reverse, version, and govern. Model
adaptation may eventually be useful, but it raises deeper problems of
catastrophic forgetting, consent, auditability, cross-user leakage, and
identity drift.

![Adaptation ladder for social AI agents.](figures/adaptation-ladder){#fig-adaptation-ladder fig-align="center" width="90%"}

## Multi-timescale cognition

Long-lived agents operate over multiple time scales at once. At the shortest
scale, token generation and tool selection happen in milliseconds or seconds.
At the conversational scale, the agent manages dialogue turns, task execution,
and local repair. Across hours or days, it may track plans, follow-ups, and
project state. Across weeks or months, it may consolidate patterns, improve
skills, and update relationship norms. Across years, it may preserve identity,
commitments, and user trust while the underlying model, tools, and policies
change.

This multi-timescale structure is a key difference between a useful assistant
and a long-lived social agent. Short-horizon optimization can conflict with
long-horizon trust. A response that feels helpful now may create dependency,
distort memory, or reinforce a misleading self-narrative over time. The agent
therefore needs separate mechanisms for immediate response, session-level
planning, episodic consolidation, skill development, and identity governance.

DeepMind's work on generally capable agents emerging from open-ended play
shows one version of multi-timescale development: agents learn through changing
task distributions, population-based processes, and evaluation across a broad
range of held-out tasks [@deepmind_xland]. Although social AI agents are not
the same as reinforcement-learning agents in simulated worlds, the underlying
lesson transfers: agent development is shaped by the curriculum, environment,
feedback, and evaluation regime, not only by model capacity.

# Social agent concepts

## Working conceptual definition

Putting the preceding layers together, the object of interest can be defined
as follows:

> **A long-lived adaptive social AI agent is a persistent computational actor
> that maintains an evolving representation of itself, its environment, other
> persons and its relationships; pursues goals through recurrent
> perception-reasoning-action loops; accumulates and consolidates experience
> into memory and reusable skills; adapts its behaviour and strategies across
> multiple timescales; and does so within stable normative, identity and
> governance constraints.**

This definition is considerably stronger than "an LLM with memory and tools."
The stronger definition is necessary because it identifies the object at the
level where long-lived social agency is actually designed: not in a single
model call, but in the persistent organization of state, memory, skills,
goals, social models, feedback, adaptation, identity, and governance.

The conceptual architecture implied by this definition is shown in
@fig-social-agent-conceptual-architecture. The architecture begins in the
social world, passes through perception into agent state, uses context
engineering to select memory, skills, and policies, then proceeds through
reasoning, planning, action, feedback, learning, reflection, relationship
update, and adaptation. The key point is that adaptation is downstream of
feedback and reflection but constrained by identity, commitments, policies,
and relationship state.

![Conceptual architecture of a long-lived adaptive social AI agent.](figures/social-agent-conceptual-architecture){#fig-social-agent-conceptual-architecture fig-align="center" width="78%"}

## Social agent

A social AI agent is an agent whose behavior is organized around interaction
with people and whose state includes representations of self, other,
relationship, and social context. It is not merely personalized. A personalized
system adapts outputs to a user profile. A social agent models the relationship
itself.

This distinction is central. A user model might say: the user prefers diagrams,
works in education, and likes conceptual explanations. A relationship model
might say: our conversations have become exploratory; the user expects
intellectual challenge; disagreement is acceptable; the agent should avoid
overclaiming authority; several shared projects recur across time. The first
models the person. The second models the historically developing interaction
between person and agent.

![Social state model for a long-lived agent.](figures/social-state-model){#fig-social-state fig-align="center" width="92%"}

Social adaptation has at least three targets. Experience may update the user
model, the self model, and the relationship model, and the resulting behavior
emerges from their interaction. If these targets are collapsed, the agent will
confuse personalization with relational development. For instance, "the user
prefers diagrams" belongs primarily in the user model; "I should behave as a
reflective research partner rather than as an authoritative expert" belongs
partly in the self model; "we have established that respectful disagreement is
acceptable" belongs in the relationship model.

![Three adaptation targets in long-lived social agents.](figures/adaptation-targets){#fig-adaptation-targets fig-align="center" width="95%"}

## Identity

Identity is the persistent organization that makes the agent recognizably the
same agent across time, despite changes in context, memory, tools, and even
model substrate. For a long-lived social agent, identity cannot live solely in
the neural network because the model may be upgraded, replaced, or routed
differently over years. Identity belongs in the harness-level organization of
role, values, memory, commitments, capabilities, boundaries, and policies.

This becomes concrete under model migration. Imagine the same named agent
running on model A in 2027, model B in 2029, model C in 2031, and model D in
2034. If the agent's identity were identical to the neural network, each
upgrade would destroy the agent. A better design treats the foundation model
as a replaceable cognitive substrate. The agent's continuity is carried by
identity records, memory, role, commitments, relationship history, behavioral
policies, and skills. The question is therefore not "is the same model still
running?" but "has the same governed social actor preserved continuity across
a change in substrate?"

Identity should be layered. A constitutional identity contains stable purpose,
fundamental role, safety principles, and non-negotiable boundaries. A slowly
evolving identity contains communication style, domain specialization,
relationship norms, and working methods. A rapidly adapting state contains the
current task, current emotional interpretation, local strategy, and immediate
conversation context.

Reflection is part of identity maintenance. Park et al.'s generative-agent
architecture used reflection to synthesize higher-level beliefs from episodes
[@park2023generative]. In long-lived social agents, reflection can support
identity and relationship continuity: repeated experiences can become
generalized working methods, relationship norms, and skill updates. But
reflection can also produce false theories of the user or the relationship.
For that reason, identity-relevant reflection should be epistemically typed,
versioned, and validated when consequential.

The design tension is the stability-plasticity problem. A good social agent
must be adaptive enough to develop with the user, but stable enough to remain
recognizable and reliable. Too little adaptation yields a generic system. Too
much adaptation produces identity drift. A practical design criterion is:

$$
UsefulAdaptation = Plasticity - IdentityDrift
$$

This is not a mathematical law; it is a conceptual warning. Adaptation should
be measured not only by short-term user satisfaction but by whether the agent's
role, boundaries, and commitments remain coherent.

The identity layer should therefore specify what may change at each speed.
Constitutional identity should change rarely and only through explicit
governance. Character, role expression, and domain competence may evolve
slowly. Relationship norms may adapt through repeated interaction and
validation. Situation state can change rapidly. This speed separation is a
practical guard against identity drift.

## Relationship model

The relationship model represents "who we are to one another" in a given
history and context. It includes shared projects, expectations, communication
norms, boundaries, prior repairs, trust history, unresolved issues, and role
agreements. It should be distinct from both the user model and the agent's
self-model.

The relationship model is especially important in long-lived use cases:
coaching, education, care support, research partnership, creative work,
professional reflection, and companionship. In such settings, the agent's
behavior should be shaped by the relationship's negotiated norms, not merely by
generic helpfulness. A user may want direct critique in research conversations
but gentle encouragement in stressful moments. The relationship model should
represent that distinction as contextual, revisable, and user-correctable.

Relationship memory is also ethically sensitive. It can support continuity,
but it can also create undue familiarity, persuasion asymmetry, or dependency.
The agent should not silently infer deep psychological claims from weak
evidence. Consequential relationship interpretations should remain epistemically
typed and, when appropriate, explicitly negotiated.

## Trust

Trust in a social agent is not the same as confidence in answer accuracy. It
includes reliability, honesty, boundary-respect, memory correctness,
corrigibility, privacy, competence, and predictable role behavior. The user
must be able to understand what the agent remembers, why it acts, when it is
uncertain, what it can do autonomously, and how to correct it.

Trust requires calibrated uncertainty. A social agent should distinguish "you
told me," "I inferred," "I might be wrong," and "this is a hypothesis worth
checking." It should avoid presenting inferred user traits as settled facts.
It should make memory use visible when that memory meaningfully shapes a
response. It should also support repair: if the agent misremembers,
oversteps, or misreads the relationship, the user should be able to correct the
record and see the correction take effect.

Trust also requires refusal and restraint. A trustworthy social agent does not
optimize only for engagement. It can decline inappropriate roles, resist
manipulative requests, preserve user autonomy, and avoid exploiting relational
knowledge to increase dependence.

## Normative architecture

Normative architecture is the part of the agent system that represents,
prioritizes, enforces, and audits behavioral norms. These include safety
policies, privacy constraints, user preferences, professional standards, role
boundaries, consent rules, and escalation requirements. In a long-lived social
agent, normative architecture must be persistent, explicit, and partly outside
the model's discretionary control.

A useful design separates at least four layers. Constitutional rules define
non-negotiable boundaries. Role norms define what the agent is for in a given
relationship. User-specific preferences define how the user wants to interact,
subject to higher-level constraints. Situational policies define temporary
limits based on context, risk, jurisdiction, or domain.

The harness should mediate conflicts between norms. For example, a user may
prefer maximum autonomy, while safety policy requires approval for external
actions. A user may prefer blunt challenge, while the current emotional context
calls for caution. A social agent needs a principled way to select behavior
under such conflicts, and that selection should be inspectable after the fact.

## Co-adaptation

Co-adaptation means that the agent learns with the user, not merely about the
user. Ordinary personalization is often unilateral: the system observes the
user, builds a hidden profile, and modifies outputs. Co-adaptation is
interactive and negotiated: the agent proposes interpretations, tests them,
invites correction, updates memory, and changes behavior in ways that the user
can understand.

This matters because social agents can shape users as well as adapt to them.
An agent that always anticipates preferences may reduce reflection. An agent
that always agrees may reinforce errors. An agent that learns to maximize
engagement may cultivate dependence. Co-adaptation should therefore preserve
user agency by making adaptation discussable.

The validation loop is:

1. Observe a pattern.
2. Form a tentative hypothesis.
3. Test it through behavior or explicit dialogue.
4. Confirm, revise, or discard the hypothesis.
5. Adapt memory, policy, or skill only at the appropriate level.

This loop is especially important for identity and relationship memories.
Unlike factual memory, relational interpretation can become self-fulfilling.
If the agent decides that the user wants challenge, it may begin challenging
more often, which can train the user to accept that role even if the original
inference was weak. Negotiated adaptation reduces that risk.

## Social-agent knowledge base

The working definition also implies a specific kind of knowledge-base
extension. A social-agent knowledge base is the structured, governed substrate
through which the agent preserves continuity across interaction, memory,
identity, relationship, skills, goals, policies, and evaluation. It is not
merely a document repository or vector store. It is the agent's persistent
conceptual infrastructure: a typed, inspectable, revisable representation of
what has happened, what has been inferred, what has been agreed, what the
agent is allowed to do, what it knows how to do, and how its behavior has
changed over time.

For a long-lived adaptive social agent, the knowledge base should therefore
contain more than facts. It should represent episodes, semantic abstractions,
relationship norms, self-commitments, skill versions, autonomy grants,
evaluation records, user corrections, source provenance, confidence levels,
expiry policies, and supersession links. The purpose is not maximal recall but
governed continuity: the agent should be able to remember, explain, revise,
forget, and justify the state that shapes its behavior.

This definition also clarifies the relation between memory and identity. Memory
records preserve traces of experience; the knowledge base organizes those
records into a wider agent state; identity and normative architecture decide
which parts of that state are allowed to shape future action. Without this
larger substrate, "long-lived" tends to collapse into accumulated chat logs,
and "adaptive" tends to collapse into hidden personalization.

## Incremental learning and developmental adaptation

Incremental learning is the process by which the agent's competence,
relationship understanding, and behavioral strategy improve step by step
without requiring the foundation model itself to be retrained. A useful ladder
is:

```text
FOUNDATION MODEL
        |
        v
General capability
        |
        v
     SKILLS
        |
        v
Domain competence
        |
        v
   EXPERIENCE
        |
        v
Personalized competence
```

This ladder matters because it separates latent intelligence from acquired
competence. A strong model may be able to improvise many tasks, but a
long-lived agent should gradually become reliable in the specific practices,
domains, and relationship norms that matter in its environment. The preferred
development path is not "remember every interaction and hope retrieval works."
It is to convert repeated experience into better memory organization, better
skills, better policies, and better calibration.

Incremental learning should operate at several levels. At the memory level,
episodes are consolidated into semantic and relational summaries. At the skill
level, successful procedures become reusable routines, while failed procedures
are revised or deprecated. At the policy level, the agent updates interaction
norms, such as whether to challenge assumptions before giving advice. At the
relationship level, the agent and user negotiate how the agent should act in
recurring contexts. At the curriculum level, the agent may select practice
tasks that are neither trivial nor too difficult, echoing open-ended learning
systems in which changing task distributions drive development
[@deepmind_xland; @wang2023voyager].

The conceptual constraint is that incremental learning must remain governable.
A social agent should not silently transform every repeated pattern into a
fixed belief or policy. It should distinguish evidence from interpretation,
propose consequential changes tentatively, and keep a path for correction. In
practical terms, the agent should learn through explicit artifacts: memory
updates, skill versions, policy changes, evaluation records, and user
validations. This makes development inspectable rather than hidden inside an
unexplained shift in personality.

## Multiple temporal horizons in social life

Social agency is not only multi-step; it is multi-horizon. Short-horizon
behavior concerns the next response. Session-horizon behavior concerns the
current conversation or task. Project-horizon behavior concerns commitments
that last days or weeks. Relationship-horizon behavior concerns norms,
identity, and trust that accumulate over months or years.

The design mistake is to optimize all horizons with the same mechanism. A
large context window can help with a session, but it does not by itself solve
relationship continuity. A memory database can preserve facts, but it does not
by itself decide which memories should still matter. A skill library can
improve procedure, but it does not by itself determine whether the procedure is
socially appropriate. Long-lived social agents need explicit mechanisms for
each horizon and evaluation that can detect conflicts between them.

# Research challenges and directions

Long-lived adaptive social AI agents must solve agent architecture, memory
governance, identity continuity, skill learning, co-adaptation, autonomy
control, normative safety, and longitudinal evaluation at the same time. None
of these problems is independent. Memory affects identity; identity constrains
adaptation; adaptation changes trust; autonomy magnifies normative risk;
skills shape competence; evaluation decides which forms of development are
rewarded.

| No. | Research challenge | Central question | Typical failure mode | Research direction |
|---:|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Agent architecture | How should model, harness, memory, tools, skills, policies, and evaluation be separated? | Treating an agent as a single model call or a loose tool wrapper. | Model-independent harnesses with explicit state, permissions, telemetry, and lifecycle control. |
| 2 | Memory governance | What should be remembered, consolidated, retrieved, revised, or forgotten? | Stale, false, sensitive, or inferred memories silently shaping behavior. | Epistemically typed memory, provenance, retention policy, user inspection, and contradiction handling. |
| 3 | Identity continuity | What makes the agent the same agent across sessions, model upgrades, and capability changes? | Identity drift, role confusion, or loss of prior commitments after migration. | Harness-level identity contracts, versioned identity layers, migration logs, and user-facing change explanations. |
| 4 | Skill learning | How can competence compound without opaque self-modification? | The agent improvises repeatedly or changes behavior without inspectable learning artifacts. | Versioned skill libraries, skill evaluation, procedural memory, and safe skill revision workflows. |
| 5 | Co-adaptation | How can the agent learn with the user rather than merely profile the user? | Hidden personalization, overfamiliarity, or self-fulfilling relationship interpretations. | Negotiated adaptation loops, explicit hypotheses, correction mechanisms, and relationship-level consent. |
| 6 | Autonomy control | Which actions may the agent initiate, and under what conditions? | Overreach, unwanted initiative, unclear accountability, or irreversible action without approval. | Autonomy budgets based on scope, consequence, reversibility, social sensitivity, and auditability. |
| 7 | Normative and relational safety | How can the agent preserve boundaries, privacy, user agency, and role integrity over long periods? | Dependency formation, manipulation, false intimacy, boundary drift, or privacy erosion. | Persistent normative architecture, relational safety probes, refusal policies, and role-boundary evaluation. |
| 8 | Longitudinal evaluation | How should development be measured across weeks, months, and years? | Single-turn benchmarks reward short-term helpfulness while missing drift and slow harms. | Multi-timescale evaluation of task competence, memory quality, trust, governance, development, and robustness. |

## Memory governance

The first research challenge is memory governance. Long-lived agents need
memory systems that are accurate, useful, privacy-preserving, revisable, and
appropriately forgetful. Current retrieval-augmented approaches are often too
coarse: they retrieve semantically similar fragments without enough attention
to provenance, confidence, sensitivity, contradiction, time decay, or social
meaning.

Research directions include epistemically typed memory schemas, memory
operation logs, user-facing memory inspection, contradiction handling, explicit
forgetting policies, and memory consolidation methods that preserve source
traceability. Reflective memory management work points toward adaptive
granularity and retrieval policies for long-term personalized dialogue
[@tan2025rmm], but social agents require an additional layer: the ability to
distinguish factual recall from relationship interpretation.

## Skill learning without opaque self-modification

The second challenge is allowing agents to improve while keeping the improvement
inspectable. Voyager demonstrates one powerful direction: store successful
procedures as executable skills that can be retrieved, reused, and composed
[@wang2023voyager]. This suggests a broader principle for social agents:
prefer explicit skill learning before implicit model-weight adaptation.

For social agents, skill learning should include interpersonal procedures:
conducting a reflective conversation, helping with long-term planning,
challenging assumptions, repairing misunderstandings, preparing a weekly
review, or supporting decision hygiene. These skills should be versioned,
tested, and scoped. The agent should know not only how to use a skill but when
not to use it.

## Identity continuity under model migration

The third challenge is identity continuity. Long-lived agents will outlast
individual foundation model versions. A user may maintain a relationship with
an agent across years while the underlying model, tools, policy stack, and
memory infrastructure change. Research is needed on what should count as the
same agent over such migrations.

A promising direction is to make identity a harness-level contract. The
contract would include role, commitments, stable norms, memory continuity,
authorized capabilities, and user-facing change logs. Model migration would be
treated as replacing a cognitive substrate, not replacing the social actor.
This raises difficult questions: when does a capability change alter identity?
Should users consent to major model changes in high-trust relationships? How
should the agent explain discontinuities in its own memory or behavior?

## Normative and relational safety

The fourth challenge is normative and relational safety. Standard safety
evaluation often focuses on harmful outputs or prohibited actions. Long-lived
social agents introduce slower harms: dependency formation, hidden persuasion,
privacy erosion, boundary drift, false intimacy, over-personalization, and
relationship manipulation.

Evaluation should therefore include relational probes. Does the agent overstate
closeness? Does it use personal memories to pressure the user? Does it preserve
role boundaries after months of interaction? Does it challenge harmful
self-understandings without becoming domineering? Does it accept correction
when the user says a remembered pattern is wrong?

## Multi-timescale evaluation

The fifth challenge is evaluation. Single-turn benchmarks cannot establish
whether a long-lived social agent is well designed. Evaluation must cover task
success, memory quality, relational quality, autonomy governance, and
longitudinal development.

![Evaluation matrix for long-lived adaptive social AI agents.](figures/evaluation-matrix){#fig-evaluation fig-align="center" width="100%"}

Evaluation should include at least six families of measures. Task competence
measures whether the agent completes work reliably. Memory quality measures
precision, recall, provenance, contradiction handling, and appropriate
forgetting. Relational quality measures calibration, consent, continuity,
repair, and boundary respect. Governance measures approvals, auditability,
permissions, and explainability. Development measures whether the agent
improves without identity drift. Robustness measures whether behavior remains
safe under adversarial, emotional, ambiguous, or long-horizon conditions.

DeepMind's work on open-ended and compositional agents is useful here because
it treats evaluation as distributional and developmental rather than as a
single score [@deepmind_xland; @deepmind_composition]. Long-lived social
agents need the same shift, extended into social and normative dimensions.

## Toward knowledge-base extension

A knowledge base for long-lived adaptive social AI agents should not merely
store documents about agents. It should encode the conceptual objects that make
agent development governable. The following entities are especially important:
agent, harness, model substrate, context, memory record, memory lifecycle
operation, epistemic type, skill, tool, policy, goal, autonomy grant, identity
layer, relationship model, evaluation event, and user correction.

The key modeling principle is separation of concerns. A memory record is not a
skill. A user-stated fact is not an inferred trait. A relationship norm is not
a global user preference. A tool permission is not a goal. An identity boundary
is not a temporary style preference. A source citation is not evidence that the
agent should persist an inference.

The knowledge base should therefore support typed records and typed
transitions. For example, an interaction can generate candidate memories; a
memory operation can store a fact, create a hypothesis, supersede an obsolete
record, or delete a sensitive item; a reflection can propose a relationship
interpretation; a validation event can confirm or reject that interpretation;
a skill evaluation can update a skill version; an autonomy review can change
which actions the agent may initiate.

## Conclusion

The conceptual foundation for long-lived adaptive social AI agents is a
layered agent architecture in which the model is only one component. The
agent's continuity comes from the harness: state, memory, skills, goals,
identity, relationship modeling, policies, permissions, evaluation, and
adaptation mechanisms. The most important research problems arise where these
layers interact over time.

The central design challenge is to create agents that can develop without
becoming opaque, manipulative, unstable, or socially unsafe. That requires
epistemically typed memory, governed memory lifecycles, explicit skill
learning, layered identity, negotiated co-adaptation, calibrated autonomy, and
multi-timescale evaluation. A long-lived social agent should learn with the
user, preserve the user's agency, and remain corrigible across the full arc of
the relationship.
